summary:
Kedah stands under Malaysia's national framework: the federal Penal Code's sections 377A and 377B criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, and these provisions apply to foreign visitors as well as citizens. Section 377D's undefined offence of "gross indecency" adds up to two years as a discretionary charge. Non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone.

Kedah additionally maintains its own state criminal law through the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). Sections 23 and 24 criminalise liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex), punishable by a fine of up to RM5,000, up to three years' imprisonment, or up to six strokes of whipping, or any combination. Section 26 criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, with a fine of up to RM1,000 or up to one year's imprisonment; female cross-dressing is not criminalised under this section. These state offences apply only to Muslim persons, and enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, whose officers determine on the ground where compliant presentation ends and the offence begins.

Enforcement in Kedah has targeted transgender people directly. In October 2020 a private birthday party in Kedah was raided and 30 trans women were singled out and arrested, and a coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups expressed concern that the event organiser was then probed for "encouraging vice" — a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of transgender persons alongside trans people themselves.

Women convicted of musahaqah under Kedah's enactment may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to six months under section 52, a custodial alternative to prison prescribed by the same law.

Malaysia provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and no form of partner recognition or same-sex marriage is available. Identity-document marker changes are routinely rejected by the Registration Department, and the 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict that sex is determined at birth, though never gazetted and not legally binding, is applied in practice. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern of venue raids and mass arrests under section 377B extends to Kedah's neighbours: police raided a second sauna in Penang within days of the Home Minister's December 2025 statement that the provisions would be revisited, following the largest such raid since 2022 at a Kuala Lumpur sauna on 28 November 2025 in which 208 men were arrested. Earlier raids include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, and 11 shopping malls in May 2023.

The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence rather than on the substance; nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised, and Kedah's own enactment was not affected.

Violence against transgender women in Malaysia is lethal and largely unpunished: a trans woman was killed in Klang in June 2019, the third such killing in fewer than two months, and reporting on those killings is obstructed by investigative practices that leave police mistreatment and impunity unexamined.
localsOnly:
Kedah's Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 applies to Muslim residents of the state. Section 26's criminalisation of a male posing as a woman in public exposes trans women to arrest by the state Islamic religious department for their everyday presentation, while female cross-dressing is not an offence under the same section. The enactment contains no legal definition of transgender dress, so the boundary between lawful and offending presentation is set by officers at the point of arrest.

Women convicted of musahaqah under section 24 may be committed to an approved home for up to six months under section 52 in addition to or instead of the fine, imprisonment or whipping available under the substantive offence.

The October 2020 raid on a private birthday party in Kedah, in which 30 trans women were arrested and the organiser was subsequently probed for "encouraging vice", indicates that residents who host or organise events attended by transgender people face exposure alongside the transgender guests themselves.

Marker changes on identity documents are routinely refused by the Registration Department, and the non-gazetted 1982 fatwa that sex is fixed at birth is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people. The only successful documented marker change is historical: in 1975 the Registration Department recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim as female and the Johor Deputy Mufti permitted her to marry under Sharia law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kedah-specific incident of lethal violence against a transgender person is documented in the available sources; the killings cited (Klang, June 2019) occurred in other states and are carried as national context only.

The sources do not document whether Kedah's Islamic religious department has issued any written enforcement directive on section 26 comparable to the July 2020 Federal Territories statement granting the department "full licence" to act against transgender persons; the Kedah record rests on the October 2020 raid and probe.

Whether Kedah has pursued any prosecution under section 26 since the 2014 enactment, and the outcomes of those prosecutions, are not sourced here.

The interaction between Kedah's enactment and the federalism reasoning of the Federal Court's February 2021 and February 2024 judgments — whether Kedah's section 26 is vulnerable to a similar challenge — is unresolved in the available material.
